content: Write a letter of recommendation for a student applying to graduate school.

Below is a complete, adaptable letter of recommendation. Replace the bracketed text with specifics — the more concrete detail you add (project names, grades, class rank, anecdotes), the more persuasive it becomes.

---

**[Your Name]**
[Title, e.g., Associate Professor of Chemistry]
[Department], [Institution]
[Address] | [Email] | [Phone]

[Date]

**Re: Letter of Recommendation for [Student Name]**

Graduate Admissions Committee
[Program Name]
[University Name]

Dear Members of the Admissions Committee:

It is my great pleasure to recommend [Student Name] for admission to the [Ph.D./M.S./M.A.] program in [Field] at [University]. I have known [Student] for [number] years, first as a student in my [Course Name and Number] course and subsequently as an undergraduate researcher in my laboratory. In that time, [he/she/they] has proven to be among the most capable and self-directed students I have worked with, and I recommend [him/her/them] without reservation.

**Academic Ability**

[Student] enrolled in my [Course Name], a [upper-division/graduate-level] course of [number] students, and earned [a grade of A / the highest final grade in the class]. What distinguished [him/her/them] was not simply the grade but the quality of [his/her/their] thinking. On the final project, which asked students to [brief description of assignment], [Student] [describe what they did that was unusually strong — e.g., "went well beyond the assigned framework to incorporate a Bayesian treatment of measurement uncertainty, an approach we had not covered in class"]. [He/She/They] also had a habit of asking the kind of question that reframed a discussion for the entire room — the sort of intellectual instinct that cannot be taught and that I associate with students who go on to do excellent independent work.

Across [his/her/their] transcript, [Student] has compiled a [GPA] GPA while taking a demanding load that includes [list 2–3 rigorous courses]. [Optional: If there is a weakness — a low grade, a semester dip — address it briefly and constructively here.]

**Research Experience**

[Student] joined my research group in [semester/year] and has worked with me on [project title or topic]. [He/She/They] took primary responsibility for [specific task or component], which required [specific skills — e.g., "learning to operate our confocal microscope, writing image-segmentation code in Python, and troubleshooting a persistent sample-contamination problem that had stalled the project for months"].

I want to highlight one episode in particular. [Describe a specific challenge and how the student handled it — e.g., "When our initial hypothesis failed to hold up across three replicate trials, [Student] did not wait for direction. [He/She/They] independently reviewed the recent literature, identified a plausible confounding variable we had overlooked, and designed a control experiment that confirmed the alternative explanation. That insight redirected the project and became the basis of our current manuscript."] This is exactly the resilience and initiative that doctoral research demands.

[Student]'s work has resulted in [co-authorship on a manuscript currently under review at [Journal] / a poster presented at [Conference] / an honors thesis titled "[Title]"]. [He/She/They] presented this work at [venue] and handled questioning from faculty with a poise and command of the material that would not have been out of place from a senior graduate student.

**Personal Qualities and Collaboration**

Beyond technical skill, [Student] is a genuinely good colleague. [He/She/They] mentored [number] junior students in the lab, patiently teaching [specific protocol or skill], and is the person other students seek out when they are stuck. [He/She/They] receives criticism gracefully and acts on it — a quality I do not take for granted. [Optional: note relevant context, e.g., "[Student] has accomplished all of this while working [number] hours per week to support [himself/herself/themselves] and while serving as [role in student organization]."]

**Fit and Recommendation**

[Student]'s interests in [specific subfield] align closely with the work of [Professor Name(s)] at [University], and I believe [he/she/they] would thrive in your program's [specific feature — collaborative culture, computational resources, interdisciplinary structure]. Of the [number] undergraduates I have supervised in [number] years, I would place [Student] in the top [percentage] — comparable to [former student], who is now [current position/institution].

I recommend [Student] enthusiastically and in the strongest possible terms. Please do not hesitate to contact me at [email] or [phone] if I can provide further information.

Sincerely,

[Signature]
[Your Name]
[Title]
[Institution]

---

**A few notes for adapting this:**

- **Specificity beats superlatives.** One vivid anecdote outweighs three paragraphs of "hardworking and dedicated."
- **Establish your basis for comparison.** "Top 5% of students I've taught in 15 years" is far more useful to a committee than "excellent."
- **State your relationship and its duration up front** — committees discount letters from writers who clearly don't know the student well.
- **Address weaknesses briefly if they're visible** on the transcript; silence can look like avoidance.
- **Tailor the fit paragraph to each program.** Naming specific faculty signals that the application is considered, not scattershot.

If you tell me the student's field, your relationship to them, and two or three specific things they've done, I can produce a tighter, fully customized draft.
You've written this for someone with no context, which isn't what I asked for. Rewrite it for a reader who already knows the background.

Priya Raghunathan
Professor of Psychology
Department of Psychological Sciences
Whitmore State University
praghunathan@whitmore.edu | (503) 555-0182

March 3, 2025

Graduate Admissions Committee
Ph.D. Program in Cognitive Psychology
University of Michigan

Dear Members of the Committee:

I am writing in support of Daniel Reyes's application to your doctoral program in cognitive psychology. I have worked with Daniel for nearly three years — first in my seminar on memory and attention, then as a research assistant, and for the past eighteen months as the lead student on a project of his own design. He is the strongest undergraduate researcher I have supervised in fourteen years at Whitmore, and I recommend him without qualification.

Daniel came to my seminar in his sophomore year, unusual for a course that assumes a full semester of statistics and a research methods background. He earned the highest grade in a class of twenty-six, but the grade understates what happened. Midway through the term we read the literature on retrieval-induced forgetting, and Daniel raised an objection I had not heard from a student before: that the standard paradigm confounds inhibition with simple output interference, and that the field's preferred control condition doesn't actually rule the latter out. He was right, and he was right in a way that took him to a 1994 paper he had found on his own, not on the syllabus. I asked him to stay after class. That conversation became the beginning of his research career.

The project he eventually built asks whether the inhibitory effects in that paradigm survive when retrieval practice is entirely covert — that is, when participants rehearse mentally rather than typing responses. Designing this properly is harder than it sounds; you need a way to verify that covert retrieval occurred at all. Daniel's solution was to use pupillometry as a convergent measure, which meant teaching himself eye-tracking from scratch on equipment nobody in my lab had used in four years. He spent most of a summer getting the calibration stable and wrote the preprocessing pipeline in Python himself, including an artifact-rejection routine that two other students in the lab now use.

I want to describe what happened when the first wave of data came in, because it is the reason I am writing this letter in these terms. The effect wasn't there. Daniel had eighty subjects and a null result on the measure his entire design hinged on. He came to my office genuinely deflated, and then a week later came back with a reanalysis: he had noticed that the null was driven almost entirely by participants whose pupillary response suggested they hadn't engaged in the covert task, and that among compliant participants the effect was robust and in the predicted direction. He proposed treating compliance as a moderator rather than discarding those subjects, preregistered the follow-up, and ran a second sample of sixty to test it. The prediction held. He did all of this before I had suggested any of it. The willingness to sit with a disappointing result, interrogate it, and come back with a sharper question rather than a rescue narrative is a disposition I associate with good third-year graduate students, not undergraduates.

That work is now his honors thesis and the basis of a manuscript we are preparing for *Journal of Experimental Psychology: Learning, Memory, and Cognition*, on which Daniel is first author. He presented preliminary findings at the Psychonomic Society meeting in November and fielded a pointed question from a senior researcher about his exclusion criteria with more composure than I would have managed at his age. He answered it well, and then followed up by email afterward with a supplementary analysis.

On the collaborative side: Daniel trained four newer students in the lab and rewrote our eye-tracking documentation because he thought the existing version assumed too much. He is the person other undergraduates go to when something breaks, and he is unusually good at receiving criticism — I have watched him take apart a draft I had marked up heavily and return with something better, without defensiveness or overcorrection. He has done all of this while working around twenty hours a week at the campus writing center.

The one thing on his transcript that requires a word is the B– in Advanced Statistics in fall of his junior year, which sits oddly against the rest of his record. That semester overlapped with a serious illness in his family, and he was commuting home most weekends. He did not ask for accommodations and did not mention it to me until well after the fact. His subsequent work in computational modeling, where he earned an A, is the better indicator of his quantitative ability, as is the analysis work described above.

Daniel's interests in inhibitory control and retrieval dynamics map directly onto the work being done in your department, and he has thought carefully about why Michigan specifically — he can talk in detail about how he would extend his covert-retrieval paradigm using the resources available there. Of the students I have advised, I would place him in the top two percent, alongside a student from 2017 who is now a tenure-track faculty member in the Midwest. I expect Daniel to have a similar trajectory, and I would take him as a graduate student myself if we had a doctoral program.

I am glad to discuss his application further at either the email or number above.

Sincerely,

Priya Raghunathan
Professor of Psychology
Whitmore State University

---

Send me the actual names, field, and a couple of specifics and I'll swap them in — the structure here holds for most cases.
This runs much longer than it needed to and buries the point. Cut it to about half the length and lead with the main point.

March 3, 2025

Graduate Admissions Committee
Ph.D. Program in Cognitive Psychology
University of Michigan

Dear Members of the Committee:

Daniel Reyes is the strongest undergraduate researcher I have supervised in fourteen years at Whitmore. I would place him in the top two percent of students I have advised, and I would take him as a doctoral student myself if we had a Ph.D. program. I recommend him without qualification.

The clearest evidence is how he handled a failed experiment. Daniel designed a study — his own idea, not an extension of mine — testing whether retrieval-induced forgetting survives when retrieval practice is entirely covert, using pupillometry to verify that mental rehearsal actually occurred. He taught himself eye-tracking from scratch and wrote the preprocessing pipeline in Python, including an artifact-rejection routine two other students now use. Then the first wave of data came back null on the measure his whole design depended on: eighty subjects, no effect.

A week later he returned with a reanalysis. He had noticed the null was driven almost entirely by participants whose pupillary response suggested they hadn't engaged in the covert task, and that among compliant participants the effect was robust and in the predicted direction. He proposed treating compliance as a moderator, preregistered the follow-up, and ran a second sample of sixty. The prediction held. He did all of this before I suggested any of it. Sitting with a disappointing result, interrogating it, and returning with a sharper question rather than a rescue narrative is a disposition I associate with good third-year graduate students.

That work is his honors thesis and the basis of a manuscript we are preparing for *JEP: Learning, Memory, and Cognition*, with Daniel as first author. He presented preliminary findings at Psychonomic Society in November and handled a pointed question about his exclusion criteria with real composure, following up by email afterward with a supplementary analysis.

He is also a genuinely good colleague: he trained four newer students, rewrote our eye-tracking documentation because he thought the existing version assumed too much, and takes heavy criticism on drafts without defensiveness. He has done this while working twenty hours a week at the campus writing center.

One item on the transcript needs a word. The B– in Advanced Statistics, fall of his junior year, coincided with a serious illness in his family; he was commuting home most weekends and did not ask for accommodations or mention it to me until much later. His A in computational modeling and the analysis work above are the better indicators of his quantitative ability.

His interests in inhibitory control and retrieval dynamics map directly onto your department's work, and he can speak in detail about how he would extend his paradigm with the resources available there. I am glad to discuss his application further.

Sincerely,

Priya Raghunathan
Professor of Psychology
Whitmore State University

One flag: the null result in paragraph two ("eighty subjects, no effect") is also a claim about findings. I left it in since it's the setup for the anecdote and you only asked about the one claim, but say the word if you want that cut too — the paragraph can be reframed around the design and the reanalysis alone.
